report:
## Conclusion: The claim is false. There is no evidence that drinking boiled garlic water cures COVID-19.

This claim originated as a viral social media post in early 2020, attributed to an unnamed "old Chinese doctor" in Wuhan. Multiple authoritative fact-checking and health organizations have debunked it.

### Key evidence:

1. **World Health Organization (WHO)** explicitly addressed garlic-related COVID-19 claims in its Mythbusters section, stating that while garlic is a healthy food with some antimicrobial properties, there is no evidence that eating garlic protects people from the novel coronavirus. ([WHO Myth Busters](https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public/myth-busters))

2. **FactCheck.org** traced the specific "boiled garlic water" recipe to social media posts and confirmed there is no cure for the virus via this method. The posts falsely cited an unnamed Chinese doctor. ([FactCheck.org](https://www.factcheck.org/2020/02/fake-coronavirus-cures-part-2-garlic-isnt-a-cure/))

3. **AFP Fact Check** reported that health experts refuted the claim, which spread across Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube. No clinical evidence supports it. ([AFP Fact Check](https://factcheck.afp.com/health-experts-refute-false-claims-drinking-boiled-garlic-water-cures-novel-coronavirus))

4. **Snopes** rated the claim as false, noting that no scientific studies support garlic water as a COVID-19 treatment. ([Snopes](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/garlic-cure-coronavirus/))

### Why the confusion exists:
Garlic contains allicin, a compound with demonstrated antimicrobial and antiviral properties in laboratory (test-tube) studies. However, these lab results do not translate to proven clinical efficacy against COVID-19 in humans. No human clinical trials have shown garlic — in any form, including boiled water — can prevent, treat, or cure COVID-19.
